title: Information Structures
body:
Information Structures is about the containers a program keeps its data in and what each one charges for
reaching that data. First year built a [[Linked List]] and a [[Stack]] by hand and stopped
there. This course builds six containers, measures every operation on each, and turns the
measurements into a decision procedure.

The containers are the [[Stack]], the [[Queue]], the [[Tree]], the [[Heap]], the
[[Hash Map]] and the [[Graph]]. All six hold the same data. They differ in which operation is
fast and which is slow, and no structure is fast at everything, so choosing one means deciding
which operation the program performs most.

The habit the course builds is pricing an operation before choosing the structure that
performs it. That habit runs for the rest of the degree: [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] is assembled
from these structures in the [[Ready Queue]] and the [[Linked List]] of process control
blocks, and [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] continues the analysis this course begins.

## Topics

### The interface and the implementation

An [[Abstract Data Type]] states which operations exist and says nothing about how they work.
A data structure implements those operations and determines what each one costs. The two are
separate questions, and keeping them separate is what allows a program to swap one structure
for another without changing the code that uses it.

A stack is the standard illustration. As an ADT it holds items, `push` adds one and `pop`
removes the most recently added one. That description works whether the items sit in an
[[Array]] or in a chain of nodes, and those two implementations have different costs.

### Measuring cost

[[Asymptotic Analysis]] answers the question of what fast means with no stopwatch involved. It
counts how the work grows as the input grows and discards constant factors, because a constant
factor changes with the machine and the growth rate does not.

```java
// O(n): one pass, work proportional to the length
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    sum += a[i];

// O(n²): a pass inside a pass
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
        if (a[i] == a[j]) count++;
```

At $n = 1000$ the first loop performs 1000 operations and the second performs 1000000. The
gap widens with $n$, which is why the growth rate settles the comparison and the constant
factor does not. [[Time Complexity]] records the results for each structure and [[Algorithm]]
covers what is being measured. Every course after this one assumes the notation.

### The language

[[Java]] replaces the C++ of first year, and the memory rules change with it. Atomic
[[Data type|data types]] are always passed by value and objects are always passed by
reference, so the choice C++ offered through [[Call by value]] and [[Call by reference]]
disappears along with the `&` operator. [[Array|Arrays]] are objects created with `new`, and a
two-dimensional array is an array of arrays, so its rows can have different lengths. Java also
collects garbage, which removes the `delete` that C++ required and the leak that follows a
missing one.

### Arrays and linked lists

These two are the foundation, and every later structure is built from one of them.

An array holds its elements in one continuous block of memory. Reaching element $i$ is
arithmetic, since the address is the start plus $i$ times the element size, so access costs
$O(1)$ regardless of the index. Inserting at the front costs $O(n)$, because every later
element shifts up one position to make room.

A [[Linked List]] holds each element in its own node alongside a pointer to the next node.
Reaching element $i$ means following $i$ pointers, so access costs $O(n)$. Inserting at the
front costs $O(1)$, because it allocates one node and adjusts one pointer.

| Operation | Array | Linked list |
|---|---|---|
| Access element $i$ | $O(1)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Insert at front | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ |
| Insert at back | $O(1)$ amortised | $O(1)$ with a tail pointer |
| Memory per element | the value | the value plus a pointer |

The two rows in the middle reverse, which is the whole comparison. [[Dynamic Arrays]] resolves
the size problem by allocating a larger block and copying when the current one fills, usually
doubling. A single append that triggers a resize costs $O(n)$, and the copies are rare enough
that the average across many appends is $O(1)$, which is called amortised cost.
[[Dynamic Data Structure]] covers growth at run time generally.

### Stacks and queues

A [[Stack]] is last in, first out. Both `push` and `pop` act at the same end, so both cost
$O(1)$ on either implementation. It is the structure behind function calls, undo history and
matching brackets.

A [[Queue]] is [[FIFO]], first in first out, with `enqueue` at the back and `dequeue` at the
front. On a linked list with a tail pointer both cost $O(1)$. On an array a naive
implementation shifts everything on each dequeue, which costs $O(n)$, and the fix is a
circular buffer where two indices chase each other around a fixed array.

```
stack:  push 1, push 2, push 3, pop  ->  3      (last one added)
queue:  enq  1, enq  2, enq  3, deq  ->  1      (first one added)
```

### Trees

A [[Tree]] holds each element in a node with links to several children, and the shape is what
makes it useful. A [[Binary Search Tree]] gives each node at most two children and maintains
one invariant: every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and every key in the
right subtree is larger.

```
          50
        /    \
      30      70
     /  \    /  \
   20   40  60   80
```

Searching for 60 compares against 50, goes right, compares against 70, goes left, and arrives.
Each comparison discards an entire subtree, so a search on a tree of height $h$ costs $O(h)$.
Insertion follows the same descent and hangs the new node where the search fell off the
bottom. An in-order traversal, meaning left subtree, then node, then right subtree, emits the
keys in sorted order, which is a free consequence of the invariant.

The height is the catch. On a balanced tree $h = \log_2 n$, so a tree of a million keys is 20
levels deep and a search touches 20 nodes. Insert already-sorted data and every new key hangs
off the right of the previous one:

```
   20
     \
      30
        \
         40
           \
            50          h = n, and search is now O(n)
```

That is a [[Linked List]] with extra pointers. A [[Balanced Tree]] prevents it by rotating
subtrees during insertion to bound the height difference between siblings, which restores the
$O(\log n)$ guarantee at the cost of extra work per insertion.

A [[Heap]] applies a weaker ordering to a different question. It is a complete binary tree
where every parent compares correctly against its children, and no relationship is required
between siblings. That is enough to keep the extreme value at the root, so reading the minimum
costs $O(1)$, while inserting and removing the minimum cost $O(\log n)$ because a value moves
along one path to restore the property. A heap is what a priority queue is built from, and it
answers "what is the smallest" without answering "what is the order".

### Hashing

Searching a tree costs $O(\log n)$ because it compares. A [[Hash Map]] avoids comparing at
all. A [[Hash Function]] converts a key directly into an array index, so the value is reached
by computing where it must be.

```java
index = hash(key) % tableSize;      // key "Evan" -> 7, look in slot 7
```

That costs $O(1)$ on average, which beats every comparison-based structure. Two costs come
with it. The first is collisions, where two keys produce one index, resolved by chaining the
entries in a list at that slot or by probing for another slot. In the worst case every key
collides and lookup degrades to $O(n)$. The second is order: a hash table has none, so
producing the keys in sorted order requires sorting them, and a [[Binary Search Tree]] gives
that away for free.

Table sizes are often a [[Prime Number]], which spreads keys more evenly when the hash
function has a periodic pattern, since a composite size shares factors with any pattern that
matches one of its divisors. [[Hashing]] and [[Maps]] cover the general technique.

### Graphs

A [[Graph]] is a set of [[Vertices]] with edges between them, and it is the most general
structure in the course, since a tree is a graph with no cycles and a list is a graph where
every vertex has one neighbour. A [[Directed Graph]] gives edges a direction, and a
[[Weighted Graph]] gives them a cost.

Two representations, for the same four-vertex graph:

```
edges: A-B, A-C, C-D

adjacency matrix              adjacency list
    A  B  C  D                A -> B, C
A [ 0  1  1  0 ]              B -> A
B [ 1  0  0  0 ]              C -> A, D
C [ 1  0  0  1 ]              D -> C
D [ 0  0  1  0 ]
```

An [[Adjacency Matrix]] uses $O(V^2)$ space and answers "is there an edge from A to D" in
$O(1)$ by one lookup. An [[Adjacency List]] uses $O(V + E)$ space and answers the same
question by scanning one list. A dense graph suits the matrix, and a sparse graph, where most
of the matrix would be zeros, suits the list.

A [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] visits every vertex exactly once and returns to its start. Finding one
is the first problem in the course with no known efficient algorithm, and checking a proposed
one takes a single pass. That gap is the entry point to [[NP-Complete]] and
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]].

### Sorting

| Sort | Average | Worst | Properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[Bubble Sort]] | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n^2)$ | teaching example only |
| [[Insertion Sort]] | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n)$ on nearly sorted input, fastest option for small $n$ |
| [[Merge Sort]] | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n \log n)$ | stable, requires $O(n)$ extra space |
| [[Quick Sort]] | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n^2)$ | sorts in place, degrades on a bad pivot |

[[Merge Sort]] splits the array in half, sorts each half by the same method, and merges the
two sorted halves in one pass. The splitting produces $\log_2 n$ levels and each level merges
$n$ elements, giving $n \log n$ with no dependence on the input arrangement.
[[Quick Sort]] partitions around a chosen pivot and recurses on each side, which needs no
extra array and produces two pieces of unequal size, so an unlucky pivot on every step gives
$n$ levels and $O(n^2)$.

No comparison sort beats $O(n \log n)$ in the worst case. There are $n!$ possible orderings,
each comparison has two outcomes and therefore halves the candidates at best, so
distinguishing them takes at least $\log_2(n!)$ comparisons, which is $\Theta(n \log n)$.
Production sorts combine the table above, running quicksort over the bulk of the array and
switching to insertion sort once a partition drops below a size threshold, where the smaller
constant factor wins.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] is where [[Pointer|pointers]],
  [[Linked Structure|linked structures]], [[Recursion]] and [[Data Structure]] first appear.
  This course is the direct continuation and adds the cost analysis.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] continues the analysis half and treats [[Time Complexity]]
  and [[NP-Complete]] in full, along with the algorithms that run over these structures.
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] builds the kernel from them, in the [[Ready Queue]], the
  [[Wait Queue]], the [[Linked List]] of [[PCB|PCBs]], the [[Stack]] and the [[Heap]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] explains why [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] is hard
  and why $\log n$ bounds a comparison-based search.
- [[DISCRETE MATH]] supplies [[Sets]], [[Proof By Induction]] for proving a
  recursive structure correct, and [[Combination]] and [[Permutation]] for counting a search
  space, including the $n!$ in the sorting bound.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] uses the same Java from the design
  side, in the [[Object Oriented Approach]], [[Inheritance]] and [[Polymorphism]].
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] explains the prime table size, since $\mathbb{Z}_p$ has no
  divisors to share with a periodic key pattern.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] covers this ground again in [[Minimum Spanning Tree]],
  [[Search Trees]] and [[Sequential Sorting]].
